content: Starch, with the chemical formula (C6H10O5)n and CAS number 9005-25-8, is a polymer of glucose composed of two main components: amylose and amylopectin. These two polysaccharides are typically present in a ratio of 20:80 or 30:70. Glucose, the monomeric unit of starch, has the chemical formula C6H12O6. The structure of starch, regardless of the amylose-to-amylopectin ratio, classifies it as a glucose polymer. In human nutrition, starch is the most widely consumed polysaccharide and constitutes a significant portion of dietary carbohydrates. In many diets, particularly in less affluent regions, starch provides the majority of caloric intake. Staple foods such as cereals, roots, and tubers are primary sources of dietary starch. Starch, especially cornstarch, is commonly used in cooking as a thickening agent for sauces and other dishes. Beyond its culinary applications, starch is utilized industrially in the production of adhesives, paper, textiles, and as a mold for manufacturing confectionery items like jelly beans and wine gums. It is typically a white, tasteless, and odorless powder, derived from plant sources such as fruits, seeds, rhizomes, or tubers. These plant-derived starches serve as an energy source when consumed. Globally, the primary sources of starch production and consumption include rice, wheat, corn, and potatoes. Cooked starch-rich foods include boiled rice, bread, noodles, and pasta. Other starches used in food processing include arrowroot and tapioca. Additional starch sources worldwide include arracacha, buckwheat, banana, barley, cassava, kudzu, oca, sago, sorghum, sweet potato, taro, and yams. Legumes such as fava beans, lentils, and peas are also rich in starch. Pregelatinized starch, which has been pre-cooked, can thicken cold foods, while raw starch requires heat to gelatinize and thicken. The gelatinization temperature varies depending on the starch type. Modified food starches, which undergo chemical modifications, are designed to withstand high heat and mechanical shear during food processing. These starches are commonly used as thickeners and stabilizers in products like puddings, custards, soups, sauces, gravies, pie fillings, and salad dressings. Resistant starch, a type of starch that resists digestion in the small intestine, has gained attention for its potential health benefits. Plants store excess glucose as starch, which serves as an energy reserve during mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. In non-food applications, starch plays a significant role in papermaking, which is the largest global non-food use of starch. Millions of metric tons of starch are consumed annually in this industry. In the wet-end phase of papermaking, cationic starches (chemically modified to carry a positive charge) interact with negatively charged paper fibers and fillers, providing wet strength to the paper web and dry strength to the final sheet. In the dry-end phase, enzymatically or chemically depolymerized starch paste is applied to the paper web, enhancing its strength and improving water resistance for better printing properties. Starch is also a key component in corrugating glues used for manufacturing corrugated fiberboard (cardboard). These glues, made from partially gelatinized starches, bond the fluted interior paper to the outer layers, providing strength and rigidity to cardboard boxes after drying under high heat. In the construction industry, starch is used in the production of wallboard. It acts as an adhesive, binding the gypsum core to the heavyweight paper layers, and contributes to the rigidity of the final product. In laundry applications, starch is used to stiffen fabrics, a practice that dates back to the 16th and 17th centuries in Europe. Starch was historically applied to collars, cuffs, and petticoats to provide a crisp appearance and protect the fabric from dirt and sweat, which adhered to the starch and washed away easily. Starch is also used in the production of biodegradable packing peanuts, ceiling tiles, and anti-set-off spray powders in the printing industry. Additionally, starch is employed in the manufacture of bookbinding glues and can be used as a substrate for hydrogen production. In the confectionery industry, starch is used as a mold for gummed sweets like jelly beans and wine gums. A tray filled with starch is leveled, and a positive mold is pressed into the starch to create impressions. The candy mixture is poured into these impressions and allowed to set in a stove, reducing the need for traditional molds. Starch solutions are also used in chemical testing, particularly for detecting iodine. When iodine is present, the solution turns blue-black due to the formation of a starch-iodine complex, where iodine molecules fit into the helical structure of amylose. A standard starch indicator solution is prepared by dissolving 4 grams of soluble starch in 1 liter of heated water, which is then cooled before use. This complex is unstable at temperatures above 35°C and is commonly used in redox titrations. Under polarized light microscopy, starch granules exhibit a characteristic Maltese cross pattern, also known as birefringence. Starch can be hydrolyzed into simpler carbohydrates through the action of acids, enzymes, or a combination of both. Hydrolyzed starch products include maltodextrin (DE 10–20), used as a filler and thickener; corn syrups (DE 30–70), used as sweeteners and thickeners; dextrose (DE 100), which is pure glucose; and high-fructose syrup, produced by enzymatically converting glucose to fructose. High-fructose corn syrup is widely used in sweetened beverages in the United States due to its higher sweetness compared to glucose, allowing for reduced sweetener usage.
